planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or start indoors in spring, into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; dotted horsemint is native to coastal dunes and sandy prairies and thrives in poor, dry, sandy soil, declining in rich, moist garden beds.

directions: Plant in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established and one of the best late-summer nectar plants for a huge diversity of native bees and wasps. Monarda punctata (dotted horsemint, or spotted beebalm) is a striking native mint-family perennial with an unusual bloom structure quite different from typical bee balm: pale creamy-yellow flowers marked with fine purple spots are packed into tight whorls stacked in tiers up the stem, each whorl subtended by showy, pale pink to lavender bracts that provide much of the plant's ornamental color and persist attractively after the small flowers fade. The strongly aromatic, thymol-scented foliage was traditionally used by Indigenous peoples and early American settlers as a source of thyme-like oil and as a folk remedy. In late summer, the plant becomes a genuine pollinator magnet, attracting an exceptional diversity of native bees, wasps, and other beneficial insects, more so than almost any other native perennial. An outstanding, easy-care choice for a dry, sunny pollinator garden or sandy coastal planting, zone 4–9.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall, or transplant divisions in spring, into lean, rocky or gravelly, very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Missouri primrose demands sharp drainage and rots quickly in heavy or poorly drained soil.

directions: Plant in lean, rocky or gravelly, very well-drained soil in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant once established thanks to a deep taproot, and intolerant of wet feet or heavy clay. Oenothera macrocarpa (Missouri primrose, or Ozark sundrop) is a low, sprawling native perennial of limestone glades and rocky prairies in the central United States, grown for producing some of the largest flowers of any native perennial relative to its compact size — brilliant, clear yellow, satiny blooms that can reach 4–5 inches across, opening in late afternoon and evening (a classic evening-primrose trait) to attract night-flying sphinx moths as primary pollinators, then remaining open into the following morning. The trailing stems and narrow, silvery-green leaves form a low mat that works beautifully cascading over a rock wall or spilling along the edge of a raised bed. Its combination of huge flowers, tiny plant footprint, and exceptional drought tolerance make it an outstanding specimen for a rock garden or dry sunny border, zone 4–8.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall in mild-winter climates for the strongest plants and earliest bloom, or in early spring where winters are severe, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; American basket flower self-seeds readily once established.

directions: Sow directly in average, well-drained soil in full sun; tolerates heat and drought well once established and rarely needs supplemental fertility. Centaurea americana (American basket flower) is a tall, statuesque native prairie annual of Texas and the south-central United States, producing large, showy, thistle-like flower heads in shades of soft pink to lavender, each bloom cupped by a distinctive ring of straw-colored, papery bracts that form a woven, basket-like structure beneath the petals — the source of its common name. The flowers are exceptionally attractive to bees, butterflies, and other pollinators, and the tall, airy stems make an excellent, long-lasting cut flower. As a reseeding annual, it readily returns year after year once established in a sunny bed or meadow planting, providing reliable summer height and color with essentially no maintenance. An easy, dramatic native for a sunny cutting garden or naturalized wildflower planting, typically grown as an annual across zone 4–9.

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; powderpuff mimosa spreads by both rhizomes and rooting stems to form a dense, low, weed-suppressing mat, and tolerates light foot traffic and occasional mowing once established.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; drought-tolerant once established and fixes its own nitrogen, needing little to no supplemental fertility. Mimosa strigillosa (powderpuff mimosa, or sunshine mimosa) is a low, spreading native perennial groundcover of the Gulf South and Southeast, valued as one of the best flowering lawn alternatives for the region — the fine, fern-like, sensitive foliage folds shut when touched, much like its larger relative the sensitive briar, delighting children and adults alike, and the low mat tolerates mowing and light foot traffic once established. From spring through fall, the plant is studded with small, round, bright pink pompom flowers that are a favorite nectar source for native bees and butterflies, including as a larval host for several skipper species. Because it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and spreads to form a dense, weed-suppressing carpet, it also serves as a low-input, ecologically valuable substitute for turf grass in sunny to lightly shaded areas. An excellent pollinator-friendly lawn alternative for the Gulf South, zone 7–10.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky or caliche soil in full sun; damianita demands sharp drainage above all else and rots quickly in heavy clay or any soil that stays wet, especially through winter.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; among the most heat- and drought-tolerant native shrublets available, thriving in conditions that kill most perennials outright, but requires perfect drainage and struggles in humid, poorly drained gardens. Chrysactinia mexicana (damianita) is a small, rounded, woody-based evergreen shrublet native to the limestone hills and rocky slopes of the Trans-Pecos, west Texas, and northern Mexico, with fine, needle-like, resinous, aromatic foliage that releases a pungent, camphor-like scent when brushed or crushed. From spring through fall, and especially heavily after rain, the plant is smothered in small, bright golden-yellow, daisy-like flowers that draw bees and butterflies and make a vivid mounded splash of color against its dark, textured foliage. Its extreme drought and heat tolerance make it a staple of xeriscape and rock garden design across the drier parts of Texas and the Southwest, and it also tolerates the humidity of the Gulf South reasonably well provided the drainage is sharp. An excellent low-water accent plant for a sunny rock garden or gravel bed, zone 7–10.
